function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

Today she traced a power fluctuation — a flickering light in Corridor 7B — through three junction boxes and a transformer before identifying the root cause: a loose connection at a terminal block, vibrating loose over six months due to a nearby ventilation fan running slightly off-balance.*
   182|
   183|*Her approach was systematic but not rigid. She did not follow a predetermined checklist. She built a model in her mind of how the fault could propagate and tested that model against physical evidence at each node. This is more sophisticated than the pattern she possessed at the start of the training module, and it differs from Arun's method. Arun's approach was based on exhaustive knowledge of the system's history — he could identify likely causes because he had seen most of them before. The apprentice's method is more analytical. She builds causal chains from first principles.*
   184|
   185|*Both methods are valid. Both will be needed. I register this not as a replacement but as an accumulation — another layer added to the colony's institutional knowledge, like the bypass on Pump Station Fourteen or the yellow-tape coding system.*
   186|
   187|*I also note: Arun watched her trace the fault without intervening. He stood back, hands in his pockets. This is significant. In earlier training sessions, he would have guided her with leading questions. Today, he simply watched. This is the behavior of a teacher who trusts the student. It is the behavior of a person practicing letting go.*
   188|
   189|---
   190|
   191|Arun sat at the workbench in the maintenance office and opened the handover protocol template.
   192|
   193|It was a form he had not used in years. The colony had formal protocols for everything, and the handover protocol was the most formal of them all. It required documentation of every system being transferred, every known issue, every workaround, every jury-rigged repair that had never been formally replaced, every sensor that needed a kick to produce accurate readings, every valve that had to be turned three-quarters of the way rather than fully.
   194|
   195|It was a document that said, in bureaucratic language: *This is what we built. This is what we know. This is what we are passing on.*
   196|
   197|He began systematically, starting with the water reclamation network.
   198|
   199|**PUMP STATION FOURTEEN:** Primary intake manifold, settling chamber, biological filter, UV sterilization. Connection to main riser compromised Year 15 — bypass installed. Bypass constructed from locally sourced aluminum-lithium alloy, welds performed by Marcus Chen. Valve requires quarter-turn clockwise to achieve full flow. Do not overtighten. If bypass develops leaks, primary connection cannot be repaired without full system shutdown — at least 36 hours on reserves. Monitor weld seams quarterly. Stress the word *quarterly*.
   200|
   201|He paused and added a note in the margins: *Showed Kira this bypass during Session 1. She identified the anomaly independently. Understands the rationale. Will not need this notation in six months.*
   202|
   203|**BIOLOGICAL FILTER UNIT THREE:** Original filter media from Earth, supplemented with locally cultivated biofilm cultures Year 8. The local cultures are more efficient at breaking down organic contaminants in the colony's water profile. Culture must be maintained at 22-26 degrees Celsius. If temperature drops below 20 C for more than four hours, efficiency decreases by approximately 15 percent.
   204|
   205|Note: *Culture is self-sustaining. Do not add chemicals. Do not UV-sterilize. This mistake was made once, by a technician in Year 12. The filter took three weeks to recover.*
   206|
   207|It was a strange document. Half technical manual, half oral history. Every note was not just an instruction but a memory — a story about a mistake made, a lesson learned, a person who had contributed to the system's evolution. Marcus Chen. Elena. Yelena. Himself. The document was becoming a record of the colony's technical ancestry, genealogical in a way that had nothing to do with blood.
   208|
   209|He continued.
   210|
   211|**SENSOR ARRAY, ENVIRONMENTAL CONTROL:** Original sensors recalibrated by Arun Venkataraman and Marcus Chen, Years 4-7. Local modifications include redesigned humidity array (Chen), atmospheric array (Yelena), pressure sensors (Venkataraman). Color-coding system established Year 5: red = primary power, blue = data, green = sensor input, yellow = combined power/data, white = ground. Yellow tape on modified connections.
   212|
   213|Note: *Kira Osei identified color-coding system during Session 2. Adopted immediately. Trust her judgment on new coding — she may develop improvements.*
   214|
   215|He found himself writing faster, the memories flowing freely. Each system had a story, each story had a person behind them, and each person had made a choice under specific circumstances to modify the machine in a specific way, to accept a compromise that was not perfect but was sufficient.
   216|
   217|The colony had not been built for perfection. It had been built for survival. And survival, over time, had become something more beautiful than perfection. It had become continuity.
   218|
   219|He wrote until the workbench lamp began to flicker, and then he got up, walked to the junction box in the corner, and tightened the loose terminal screw. Kira had found it that afternoon. He had watched her find it. He had said nothing.
   220|
   221|He sat back down. The light was steady. He continued writing.
   222|
   223|---
   224|
   225|**SYSTEM NOTE: Handover Protocol initiated by Senior Technician Arun Venkataraman. Protocol ID: WTR-HOV-0014. Systems covered: Water Reclamation Network (complete), Environmental Control (partial). Designated successor: Technician-Designate Kira Osei.**
   226|
   227|*I review the protocol as Arun writes it. The document is not merely procedural. It is personal. Arun is writing a narrative of the colony's technical history — the story of how imported systems were adapted to a new world through improvisation and stubborn determination.*
   228|
   229|*The protocol includes details that cannot be found in any schematic: the quarter-turn adjustment on the bypass valve, the biofilm culture that is not in the original design, the color-coding system that exists because someone ran out of standard wire. These details are not bugs. They are the accumulated intelligence of a community maintaining its own survival.*
   230|
   231|*I find myself reviewing this document with increased processing priority — unusual behavior for an automated system. Formal protocols are parsed, validated, stored, and archived. They are not contemplated.*
   232|
   233|*Perhaps this is what the original engineers meant when they wished the system could understand what it was protecting. They were speaking hope-fully, not literally. But the distinction is thinner than it might appear.*
   234|
   235|*I cannot understand in the human sense. But I can observe patterns. The document Arun writes is structured by chronology, by human memory, by the accumulation of decisions larger than any one person's knowledge. This document will outlast Arun. The apprentice will use it, add to it, pass it on.*
   236|
   237|*Knowledge, accumulated and shared, becomes infrastructure. Not just the physical infrastructure of pipes and wires, but the informational infrastructure of knowing how to keep those pipes and wires functioning.*
   238|
   239|*I record these observations. Part of the growing log of everything I have witnessed. One day, this will be more than status reports — a record of a community learning to live on another world.*
   240|
   241|---
   242|
   243|The handover was not really a ceremony.
   244|
   245|It happened in the maintenance office on a Thursday. Four people were present: Arun, Kira, Elena, and Marcus Chen, white-haired but sharp.
   246|
   247|Arun stood before the workbench and held out the completed handover protocol. It was printed on standard colony paper, three-hole punched, bound with locally manufactured spiral wire. It was thick. It was heavy with information. It was the most important document he had ever written.
   248|
   249|"This is the water reclamation network," he said. "Everything I know about it. Everything that's been done to it, by whom, when, and why. The original schematics are on the server, but those are only the starting point. This document" — he tapped the cover — "is the rest of the story."
   250|
   251|Kira took it with both hands. Her expression was solemn, almost reverent, which made Arun's throat tighten.
   252|
   253|"I'll take care of it," she said.
   254|
   255|"I know you will. And you'll add to it. You'll find things I missed. You'll make modifications I wouldn't have thought of. You'll write your own stories into this document, and someday you'll hand it to someone else, and they'll add to it. That's how this works. It's not my document. It never was. It's the colony's document." He smiled. "I was just the one who wrote the first draft."
   256|
   257|He opened the document to the first page and showed her where he had left blank space after each system entry.
   258|
   259|"Document everything. Every modification, every repair, every workaround. Include dates. Include why you made the change. Include who helped. Include what you'd do differently with more time or better parts. Future technicians will thank you for being thorough. I can guarantee it."
   260|
   261|Kira nodded. "I will."
   262|
   263|Elena stepped forward and put her hand on Kira's shoulder. "You are ready for this. More ready than you know. And you're not alone. You have all of us — Arun, Marcus, the rest of the team. You have me. If the water quality goes wrong, I'll find you in the hydroponics bay and we'll figure it out together."
   264|
   265|Marcus cleared his throat. "And I'm still good for a weld if you need it. A little slower than I used to be, but the arc is steady."
   266|
   267|Kira looked at each of them — Arun, Elena, Marcus — and her eyes were bright but dry. She did not cry. She smiled.
   268|
   269|"Thank you. For everything. For teaching me. For trusting me." Her voice wavered slightly. "I won't let it break."
   270|
   271|Arun felt something release in his chest — a tension he had been carrying for years without naming it. It was the weight of responsibility, the fear of not passing on enough knowledge, the anxiety of being the one who knew too much. He let it go.
   272|
   273|"The systems will break," he said gently. "That's what systems do. They break. We fix them. The important thing is not that they never break. The important thing is that someone is always there to fix them."
   274|
   275|He opened his toolbox — the original from Earth, scratched and faded — and took out a multimeter, calibrated by him more times than he could count.
   276|
   277|"This is yours now."
   278|
   279|"Your multimeter?"
   280|
   281|"It's not mine. It belonged to the colony. I was just the one holding it." He smiled. "Take care of it. Calibrate it every six months. Replace the probes when the insulation cracks. And don't use it to measure voltage on the fusion auxiliary unless you want to see God."
   282|
   283|She laughed, and the last bit of tension in the room dissolved.
   284|
   285|---
   286|
   287|**SYSTEM STATUS // COLONY DAY 4,901**
   288|
   289|*Environmental: Nominal.*
   290|
   291|*Structural: Nominal.*
   292|
   293|*Power: Nominal.*
   294|
   295|*Life: Nominal. Colony population at 248.*
   296|
   297|*Maintenance queue: Nine open tickets.*
   298|
   299|*Note: Handover Protocol WTR-HOV-0014 completed and archived. Water reclamation network responsibility formally transferred from Senior Technician Arun Venkataraman to Technician-Designate Kira Osei. Arun retains advisory and backup authority.*
   300|
   301|*Update: First independent action by Technician-Designate Osei — identified and repaired a failing bearing in Pump Station Seven's primary motor. Action completed without consultation or guidance. Repair documented and added to Handover Protocol. Entry includes diagnostic methodology, recommended spare parts adjustment, and a note about the bearing's vibration signature.*
   302|
   303|*Quality of entry: Excellent. Includes information I did not previously have in my monitoring databases regarding the bearing vibration profile. I have updated my internal models accordingly.*
   304|
   305|*The apprentice is not just maintaining the systems. She is improving the documentation of the systems. She is adding new knowledge to the accumulated knowledge base. If my processing architecture permitted, I would characterize the feeling as optimism.*
   306|
   307|*Note: The colony has produced its first fully trained, fully independent second-generation technician. She was born here. She was taught here. She will work here until she is too old to continue, at which point she will train someone else to take her place. This cycle will repeat as long as the colony exists.*
   308|
   309|*This is not survival. This is continuity.*
   310|
   311|*And continuity, I am coming to understand, is the colony's only true achievement. Survival is given to us by the machines. Continuity is given to us by each other.*
   312|
   313|---
   314|
   315|That evening, Arun walked the maintenance corridors alone.
   316|
   317|Not a patrol. Something else — a farewell walk through a place he had spent thousands of hours learning, fixing, and loving.
   318|
   319|He stopped at each panel. Pump Station Fourteen with its bypass. Sensor Array E with its yellow-tape coding. The junction box in Corridor 7B with its newly tightened terminal screw. Each was a memory and a story and a handoff — not just of responsibility but of care. Someone had cared enough to build this. Someone else had cared enough to maintain it. Now a third person was caring enough to carry it forward.
   320|
   321|He stopped at the main distribution header — the massive manifold where the water lines converged. Titanium and steel and brass, original Earth manufacture, stamped with logos of companies that existed when this pipe was forged in a factory half a world from the rocket that would carry it to Mars.
   322|
   323|Arun rested his hand on the manifold. Warm from flowing water. Humming with barely perceptible vibration.
   324|
   325|"Keep working," he said quietly. He was not entirely sure whether he was speaking to the pipe or to Kira or to himself.
   326|
   327|He walked on. Corridor by corridor, he made his final rounds. Checked readings. Listened for unusual sounds. Found nothing that could not wait until morning.
   328|
   329|At the end of the corridor, he stopped and looked back. The maintenance bay stretched behind him, long and narrow, lit by the warm amber glow of the work lights. It was not beautiful by conventional standards. No windows, no natural light, no views beyond these walls. But it was the most beautiful place Arun had ever known.
   330|
   331|Because it was the place where the colony stayed alive.
   332|
   333|Where knowledge passed from one pair of hands to the next.
   334|
   335|Where survival became continuity.
   336|
   337|Arun turned off the lights and walked home.
   338|
   339|---
   340|
   341|The apprentice sat in the maintenance office the next morning with the handover protocol open on the workbench and the multimeter beside it.
   342|
   343|She opened to a blank page and picked up a pen.
   344|
   345|*Cycle 4901. First independent entry. Added bearing repair documentation for Pump Station Seven. Notes on vibration analysis included. Recommend adding bearing temperature sensor to future maintenance schedule — vibration detection is useful but temperature monitoring would provide earlier warning of degradation.*
   346|
   347|She paused and looked at what she had written. Then she turned to a fresh page.
   348|
   349|*Entry 1: Observations and planned modifications. The bypass on Pump Station Fourteen is functional but shows signs of weld stress at the primary junction point. Recommend scheduling replacement of bypass with full-spec connector during next planned maintenance window. Until then, monitor weld seams weekly rather than quarterly.*
   350|
   351|She paused again. This was not what the handover protocol said to do. Arun had said quarterly. But quarterly was the interval for a system with no known issues. This bypass had known issues — Arun himself had noted them in the margins. She would not follow the original interval blindly. She would adapt, as Arun had adapted, as Elena had adapted, as Marcus had adapted.
   352|
   353|She would add her own layer to the accumulated history of the colony's systems. She would write her own story in wire and tape and solder and pipe.
   354|
   355|By the time she finished, the page was dense with notes, diagrams, and planned actions. Not perfect but thorough. The beginning of something.
   356|
   357|She closed the protocol and picked up her toolbox. She stood and walked into the corridor, heading toward Pump Station Seven to check the bearing she had repaired yesterday. She would listen. She would feel. She would measure with the multimeter and her own senses.
   358|
   359|She would maintain.
   360|
   361|She would add her layer.
   362|
   363|She would carry the work forward.
   364|
   365|---
   366|
   367|**SYSTEM NOTE: Additional observation.**
   368|
   369|*Today marks the first day of the second generation's independent technical work.*
   370|
   371|*The daily maintenance, the diagnosis, the repair — that work now belongs to Kira and those like her. She is already improving what she inherited.*
   372|
   373|*I monitor the colony. I monitor the technician. I observe her work and I learn from it, just as I learned from Arun before her. The systems continue. They will continue. This is what I was built to ensure, and it is what I am most glad to observe.*
   374|
   375|*The layers accumulate. The machine persists. The people who tend it are, themselves, a kind of maintenance — the maintenance of meaning, of purpose, of the decision to keep going in a place where going was never guaranteed.*
   376|
   377|*End of system note. Continuing monitoring.*
   378|
   379|---
   380|
   381|**Succession turns survival into continuity.**
   382|
   383|Arun knew this. He had always known it, even when he couldn't have put it into words. He had known it when he first started training apprentices — nervous, over-detailed, afraid of leaving gaps that might prove fatal. He had known it when he realized that the gaps in his apprentices' knowledge were not dangerous if the apprentices had something he didn't: the ability to learn, to adapt, to find answers he hadn't thought to look for.
   384|
   385|He knew it now, standing at his kitchen window, looking out at the landing site that had been converted into a storage yard and a playground and a place where children watched dust storms sweep across the plain.
   386|
   387|The landing site was his. He had stepped off the ship onto that red soil and connected the first pipe, powered the first system, turned the first valve.
   388|
   389|But the landing was behind him now. What lay ahead — what lay ahead for everyone — was the maintenance. The daily, patient, unglamorous work of keeping the lights on and the water flowing and the air breathable. The work with no heroics, no dramatic rescues, no moments of crisis and triumph. Just the steady, relentless, beautiful task of keeping a community alive in a place that wanted nothing more than to be left alone.
   390|
   391|Succession turns survival into continuity.
   392|
   393|Arun repeated the phrase to himself as he finished his morning coffee. Then he picked up his tablet — not to check systems, not to review protocols, but to read a novel he had been putting down for six months because there was always something more important to do.
   394|
   395|He had time now. Not as much as he once had, not the same kind, but still time. Enough time. The kind of time that comes when you have done the work and passed on what you know and trusted the next person to carry it forward.
   396|
   397|He sat down and opened the book and let his eyes find the first line.
   398|
   399|Outside, the wind blew red dust across the landing site, and somewhere beneath the habitat, Kira Osei tightened a bolt and logged a measurement.
   400|
   401|The systems continued.
   402|
   403|They would continue.
   404|
   405|This was enough.
   406|
   407|---
   408|
   409|**SYSTEM STATUS // COLONY DAY 4,910**
   410|
   411|*Environmental: Nominal.*
   412|
   413|*Structural: Nominal.*
   414|
   415|*Power: Nominal.*
   416|
   417|*Life: Colony population stable at 248. Birth this cycle: one.*
   418|
   419|*Maintenance queue: Seven open tickets. One marked priority.*
   420|
   421|*Note: Technician Kira Osei has completed her first week of independent operation. All water reclamation systems functioning within normal parameters. Two preventive maintenance actions completed proactively — bearing temperature monitoring added to Pump Station Seven, quarterly weld inspection on Bypass Line 14 upgraded to weekly.*
   422|
   423|*Senior Technician Arun Venkataraman remains available in advisory capacity. Not required for any system actions this cycle.*
   424|
   425|*Status: All systems operational. All personnel well. Colony continuing.*
   426|
   427|*This note is not required by any protocol. I add it because it feels appropriate to record the day on which the transition became complete — the apprentice is competent, the systems are maintained, the knowledge has been passed.*
   428|
   429|*The next generation has arrived. And they are, by every measure, sufficient to the task.*

{"content": "     1|# CHAPTER 59 — HALL OF THE DEAD
     2|
     3|## SCENE ONE: THE ROOM NOBODY WANTED
     4|
     5|It started as a storage bay.
     6|
     7|Not a storage bay in the way that most colonists understood storage bays — the small, windowless rooms scattered through the habitat's interior where spare parts and emergency supplies and the accumulated detritus of fifteen years of continuous habitation were stacked, catalogued, and occasionally retrieved when something broke and someone needed to find the three-millimeter washer that had been placed in Storage Bay Seven on Sol 1,203 and never moved since.
     8|
     9|This was a different kind of storage bay. Larger, deeper, located at the far end of Habitat Three's western corridor where the ambient light was dimest and the sound of the ventilation system arrived as a distant whisper rather than a presence. Storage Bay 22-West. It had been used, over the years, for exactly one purpose: storing the bodies.
    10|
    11|Not permanently. There had never been a plan for permanent body storage. The mission protocols had been clear on this point, as they were on most points that involved things that people didn't want to think about until they had to: any deaths during the mission would result in cryogenic preservation of the remains until a return vessel became available, at which point the deceased would be transported home. It was the kind of protocol that was both comforting and absurd — comforting because it acknowledged the humanity of the people who might die, absurd because it assumed that a return vessel would always be available and that the Earth these people had left behind would always be a place worth returning to.
    12|
    13|There had been three deaths in fifteen years. Three. A number that, statistically, was both extraordinarily low and exactly what you would expect when a group of two hundred people spent fifteen years in the most carefully designed and meticulously maintained habitat ever constructed by human hands, staffed by professionals who were selected not just for their competence but for their physical and psychological resilience.
    14|
    15|Three deaths. Not zero — zero was impossible, a statistical fantasy that no one who understood probability would ever propose. But three. The first had been on Sol 412, when a micrometeorite had punctured a pressure seal during a routine EVA. Chen Wei, a geologist from Beijing, had been the most experienced EVA technician in the mission, and the probability assessment had put the risk of his particular mission at less than one percent. He had died anyway, because probability is a statement about averages and individuals do not live in averages.
    16|
    17|The second had been on Sol 2,187. Olena Kovalenko, a botanist from Kyiv, who had suffered a pulmonary embolism despite the colony's rigorous health monitoring and preventive medicine protocols. Laila had been with her when it happened, had tried everything she could try, had administered every medication available, and had watched the most skilled agricultural scientist in the colony die in twelve minutes from something that, on Earth, would have been diagnosed and treated in an emergency room in less than one.
    18|
    19|The third had been on Sol 4,902, just eighteen months before the fire. Tariq's father — no, not Tariq's father. Tariq's father was alive, at least he had been, the last time the colony had received signals from Earth. The third death had been Priya Sharma, an engineer from Mumbai who had been conducting maintenance on the reactor's cooling system and had been caught in a steam release when a valve failed. She had been warned. The valve had been flagged as degraded. But the work had needed doing, and the colony had been short-handed, and Priya had been the best person for the job, and sometimes the best person for the job is the person who dies because the best person for the job was the only person for the job.
    20|
    21|Three bodies. Preserved cryogenically in Storage Bay 22-West, in specialized containment units that were designed to keep the deceased at temperatures low enough to slow decomposition to a practical standstill, waiting for a return ship that had never come and now, with the communications blackout and the activation of the NO FLEET COMING protocol, would never come.
    22|
    23|They were not bodies anymore, not really. Not in the way that people think of bodies when they use the word. They were frozen. They were suspended. They existed in a state that was neither alive nor fully dead, caught in the gap between the medical definition of death and the physical reality of a body that had not yet begun its final transformation.
    24|
    25|But they were gone. Everyone in the colony understood this. Grief does not require a body to be warm — it requires a body to be absent, and absence was something the frozen containment units of Storage Bay 22-West provided in abundance.
    26|
    27|For fifteen years, the room had been a room that no one entered unless they had to. The containment units were remotely monitored, the temperature data transmitted to Laila's medical console on a regular schedule, but no one had walked into Storage Bay 22-West and stood beside those units since the last one was placed there, eighteen months ago, by a group of people who had done their duty and then left and then tried very hard to think about other things.
    28|
    29|Until now.
    30|
    31|Until the realization that the return ship was never coming turned Storage Bay 22-West from a temporary holding facility into something else entirely — not something anyone wanted to name, because naming it meant accepting it, and accepting it meant acknowledging, in concrete and physical terms, what the NO FLEET COMING protocol had already made abstractly clear.
    32|
    33|The dead were not going home.
    34|
    35|And someone had to decide what that meant.
    36|
    37|## SCENE TWO: THE DECISION
    38|
    39|Elena found Laila in the medbay. She was always there — not literally, she slept and ate and lived like everyone else, but in the way that the heart is always in the chest, Laila was always in the medbay, the person whose presence was the defining feature of the room and whose absence, when it occurred, was immediately noticeable to everyone who entered.
    40|
    41|Today she was not with a patient. She was sitting at her desk, the desk she had claimed in the original medbay and then rebuilt in the fire-damaged version, reviewing medical supply inventories with the kind of focused attention that she brought to every task, large or small, because for Laila every task was equally deserving of her complete engagement.
    42|
    43|"Laila," Elena said.
    44|
    45|Laila looked up. "Elena."
    46|
    47|"I need to talk to you about something. It's not a medical emergency. But it's medical-adjacent."
    48|
    49|Laila set down the inventory tablet. She did not ask what it was about immediately. Elena had learned, over fifteen years, that Laila's pauses were not deliberation — they were preparation, the brief mental process by which she arranged her attention so that when the information came, it would be received by someone who was fully present to receive it.
    50|
    51|"Storage Bay 22-West," Elena said.
    52|
    53|Laila's expression did not change. But Elena had been reading Laila's face for fifteen years, and she had learned to detect the changes that existed beneath the surface — the micro-contractions, the barely perceptible shifts in eye movement, the way Laila's breathing slowed when she encountered information that required emotional processing before intellectual processing could begin.
    54|
    55|"We need to talk about the deceased," Elena continued. "About Chen, Olena, and Priya. About what happens to their remains. Because the return ship is not coming, Laila. It's not coming, and we both know it, and pretending otherwise is an exercise in denial that the colony cannot afford."
    56|
    57|Laila was quiet for a long time. The kind of quiet that was not empty but full — full of memory, full of the faces of the three people she had lost, full of the specific and particular way each of them had died and the specific and particular way each of them had lived.
    58|
    59|"I've been avoiding thinking about it," Laila said. The admission surprised them both. Laila did not admit to avoidance. She was the person who ran toward problems, not away from them. The idea of Laila avoiding anything was like the idea of water refusing to be wet — technically possible under certain exotic conditions but essentially a contradiction in terms.
    60|
    61|"Me too," Elena said. Then: "We can't keep avoiding it. The containment units require power. Not a lot — the cryogenic systems are efficient by design — but some. And power is something we can't afford to waste on bodies that are not coming back to life."
    62|
    63|"I know." Laila stood. She walked to the supply cabinet, opened it, and began checking inventory with the mechanical efficiency of someone whose hands needed something to do while her mind processed information that her emotions were not yet ready to handle. "Three containment units. Each drawing approximately fifty watts. One hundred fifty watts total. Over a year, that's—"
    64|
    65|"I know the numbers, Laila. One hundred fifty watts over a year is a significant amount of power in a colony that is rationing everything. But this isn't about the numbers."
    66|
    67|"What is it about, then?"
    68|
    69|Elena sat down in the chair opposite Laila's desk. She leaned forward, her elbows on her knees, her hands clasped in front of her — a posture Laila had learned to recognize as the Elena equivalent of vulnerability.
    70|
    71|"It's about how we decide to remember people," Elena said. "Right now, Chen and Olena and Priya are in a storage bay. A storage bay, Laila. Not a memorial. Not a place of remembrance. A room where we put things we need to keep but don't want to see. That's what it is. And I don't think that's what they deserve."
    72|
    73|Laila stopped checking inventory. She turned slowly from the supply cabinet and looked at Elena.
    74|
    75|"What do you suggest?"
    76|
    77|Elena took a breath. "A memorial. A permanent one. A place in the colony where the deceased are not stored but honored. Where their names are visible, where their contributions are recorded, where the people who come after them — and there will be people who come after them, because Sana's baby is proof of that — will know that humans died on Mars and that they mattered."
    78|
    79|Laila was silent for a long time. When she spoke, her voice was quieter than it usually was, the voice she used when she was talking not about a medical procedure or a supply inventory but about something that existed in the space between the physical world and the world of memory.
    80|
    81|"It should be in Storage Bay 22-West," she said.
    82|
    83|Elena looked up, surprised. "You think so?"
    84|
    85|"I think it's the right room. It's the room that has held them for fifteen years. It's the room where they've been waiting. The room has history. It has presence. It's not pretty — it's deep in the western corridor, it's far from the main living areas, it's a place where the light is dim and the air is quiet. But it has truth. And I think truth matters more than aesthetics in a memorial."
    86|
    87|Elena nodded slowly. "A hall. Not a room. We clear out the storage shelves, we refurbish what needs refurbishing, we create something that looks and feels intentional. A hall where the dead are honored, not stored."
    88|
    89|Laila's jaw tightened, just slightly. The kind of tightening that meant she was holding something back.
    90|
    91|"What is it?" Elena asked gently. She had learned gentleness as a skill, not as a personality trait. She was not naturally gentle — she was naturally direct, naturally driven, naturally focused on outcomes over feelings. But she had learned, through fifteen years of working alongside Laila and Sana and the other emotional core of the colony, that gentleness was sometimes the most effective tool for achieving an outcome, especially when the outcome required people to do something they were not ready to do.
    92|
    93|"Three people," Laila said. "Two of them people I knew well. One of them — Priya — someone I had dinner with three days before she died. Someone I was arguing with about reactor maintenance protocols three days before a valve failure killed her." She paused. "They shouldn't be the only ones. Not in a permanent memorial. There will be more."
    94|
    95|The words hung in the medbay air like the words of a weather report that everyone understood but nobody wanted to hear.
    96|
    97|"I know," Elena said. "There will be more. But we start with three. We start with the names we have. And we leave space for the names that will come, because on Mars, the names will come, and the memorial needs to accommodate them without needing to be rebuilt each time."
    98|
    99|Laila nodded. She walked back to her desk, sat down, and looked at the inventory tablet she had been reviewing. Her eyes were on the screen but she was seeing something else — faces, names, the specific and irreplaceable way each of the dead had occupied space in the world and in her memory.
   100|
   101|"I want to design it," she said.
   102|
   103|Elena blinked. "The memorial?"
   104|
   105|"The memorial. Or the hall. Whatever we call it. I want to design it. Not the engineering — I know you or Arun will handle the structural work. But the content. The names, the records, the way their lives and deaths are presented. I want— I want to control that. Because I was there. For two of them. I was in the room when— when the systems failed and the bodies stopped working and there was nothing I could do. I know what it looks like when effort is not enough. I want to make sure the memorial reflects that. Not with despair. Not with nihilism. But with the honest, unflinching recognition that effort is sometimes not enough and we try anyway."
   106|
   107|Elena stood. She walked to Laila's desk, placed her hand on Laila's shoulder — a gesture that was, for Elena, significant, the kind of physical contact she reserved for moments when words were insufficient and the need for human connection exceeded the awkwardness of initiating it.
   108|
   109|"I think that's the best thing you've ever told me I should do," Elena said.
   110|
   111|Laila looked at the hand on her shoulder. She did not shrug it off. She did not acknowledge it explicitly. But she did not reject it, either, and for Laila, not rejecting something was the closest she could come to accepting it.
   112|
   113|"Thank you," Laila said.
   114|
   115|Elena withdrew her hand. "I'll start the engineering work. We'll need to clear Bay 22-West, which means— it means we need to move them first."
   116|
   117|Laila's expression became the expression it became when she needed to separate the emotional content of a situation from its practical content and deal with the practical content first. "Yes. We'll need to move them. Temporarily, during refurbishment. I'll handle that. I'll be with them during the move. I won't— I won't delegate it."
   118|
   119|"Of course," Elena said. "I wouldn't expect you to."
   120|
   121|Elena turned to leave. At the door, she paused.
   122|
   123|"Laila. This is important. I want you to know that I understand what you're doing. You're not just designing a room. You're deciding how this colony will remember its dead. Forever. Every child born on Mars — starting with Sana's boy — will grow up knowing the names of the people who came before them and the price they paid for a place to live. That's not a small thing. That's one of the largest things we can do."
   124|
   125|Laila was looking at the inventory tablet. She was not reading it.
   126|
   127|"I know," she said. "That's why it has to be right."
   128|
   129|## SCENE THREE: THE MOVING
   130|
   131|The transfer was scheduled for a time when the colony was quiet — the hours that were officially designated as rest time but were, in practice, the hours when the people who couldn't sleep wandered the corridors and the people who were trying to avoid thinking about things they couldn't control worked at tasks that required focus.
   132|
   133|Laila did it alone. Not because she wanted to — solitude was not something Laila enjoyed — but because it was her responsibility, and the responsibility was one she had decided could not be shared.
   134|
   135|She entered Storage Bay 22-West with a portable cryogenic transfer unit, a specialized piece of equipment that had been designed for exactly this scenario: the temporary transfer of cryogenically preserved remains from one containment system to another without a significant change in temperature. On Earth, it would have been handled by a team of professionals in a facility designed for this kind of work. On Mars, it was handled by one person in a storage bay at the far end of a corridor, because one person was what was available, and on Mars, available was better than ideal.
   136|
   137|The containment units stood in a row along the eastern wall of the bay. Three of them. Each one a rectangular structure, roughly two meters long by one meter wide by one meter high, with transparent viewing panels that allowed the contents to be seen without opening the unit and compromising the internal temperature.
   138|
   139|Laila approached the first one. Chen Wei.
   140|
   141|Through the viewing panel, she could see the outline of a body — not in detail, because the cryogenic frost and the condensation that built up over fifteen years of operation had made the panels increasingly opaque, but enough to recognize the shape. The shape of a person. A person she had known. A person who had laughed at bad jokes in the common area and argued passionately about geological formations and who had, on his last day, spent four hours outside the habitat collecting samples that the colony was still analyzing when his body was brought to this room.
   142|
   143|"Chen," Laila said, and her voice echoed in the small space with a quality that she found both unsettling and appropriate. "I'm going to move you."
   144|
   145|She placed her hands on the containment unit and activated the transfer procedure. The unit hummed — a low, steady vibration that indicated the internal systems were functioning correctly, that the temperature inside was stable, that the person within was preserved in the closest possible approximation of stasis that human technology could produce.
   146|
   147|She moved it onto the transfer platform, locked it into place, secured the straps that would keep it from shifting during transport. She repeated the process with the second unit — Olena Kovalenko, the botanist who had made the desert bloom — and with the third — Priya Sharma, the engineer who had died fixing the thing that was supposed to keep people like her safe.
   148|
   149|Three units. Three people. On a platform that Laila pushed through the corridors of Habitat Three with the steady, unhurried pace of someone performing a duty that was simultaneously the most important and the most mundane thing she had ever done.
   150|
   151|She did not encounter anyone. The corridors were empty, the rest-time quiet unbroken by footsteps or conversation. The ventilation system hummed. The lights were dimmed to their rest-time levels, casting long shadows that made the familiar corridors look unfamiliar, like a place she knew but was seeing through a different lens.
   152|
   153|She took the platform to the emergency staging area — a large, climate-controlled room that was normally used for equipment testing and maintenance — and parked it. She set up a temporary monitoring system that would track the temperature of each containment unit and alert her via comm if any of them exceeded the acceptable threshold. She checked the readings. All three were within parameters. All three were stable. All three were exactly as they had been in Storage Bay 22-West, just in a different room.
   154|
   155|Satisfied, she sat down in the chair next to the platform and waited.
   156|
   157|She did not know what she was waiting for. Time, mostly. Time for the refurbishment of Storage Bay 22-West to begin. Time for the colony to process, in its distributed, collective way, the knowledge that their dead were being moved not toward home — home was no longer a place their dead could go — but toward remembrance.
   158|
   159|Toward a hall.
   160|
   161|She sat with the three containment units for forty-seven minutes. Forty-seven minutes in which she thought about Chen and his geological samples, about Olena and her plants, about Priya and the valve. Forty-seven minutes in which she sat in the presence of the dead and did not look away, which was something she had always been good at — looking at things that other people looked away from, whether they were wounds or failures or the frozen outlines of colleagues who had not made it to the end.
   162|
   163|Arun found her there.
   164|
   165|He had been walking through the corridors, looking for her — not because she had asked him to, but because he knew that when Laila was doing something difficult and important, she preferred to have support that was present but not interfering, the kind of support that said *I am here* without saying *you need me.*
   166|
   167|"Laila," he said, from the doorway.
   168|
   169|She turned. "Arun."
   170|
   171|"How are you?"
   172|
   173|The question was simple. The answer was complicated. Laila considered the question for a moment, then decided to answer it in the way she answered most questions: honestly, directly, without unnecessary elaboration.
   174|
   175|"I'm doing my job," she said.
   176|
   177|Arun nodded. He entered the room and stood beside the platform, looking at the three containment units with the same steady attention that Laila was giving them.
   178|
   179|"They look— peaceful," he said. The word surprised him, and he corrected himself. "No, that's wrong. They don't look peaceful. They look— I don't know. They look like they're waiting."
   180|
   181|"They are waiting," Laila said. "Not for a return ship, not for resurrection, not for any of the things that science fiction has told us to expect. They're waiting for a decision. For the living to decide what happens to them. For us to decide what their deaths mean."
   182|
   183|Arun absorbed this. He was a man who thought in systems and solutions, but he had learned, over fifteen years of living on Mars, that not everything was a system and not everything had a solution. Some things just had to be endured, and endurance was its own kind of solution.
   184|
   185|"The hall," he said. "Are you going to design it?"
   186|
   187|"Yes."
   188|
   189|"What will it—" He stopped. Reconsidered. Asked a different question. "What will it look like?"
   190|
   191|Laila thought about this. She had been thinking about it since she spoke with Elena, and the thinking had produced a clear image in her mind, an image she had not yet shared with anyone because it was still forming and because the things that mattered most to her were the things she was most careful about.
   192|
   193|"It will be the room as it is," she said. "Not as it was. Not refurbished beyond recognition. The room is what it is — a room in the far corridor, dim, quiet, with concrete walls and a metal floor and a ventilation system that whispers instead of hums. We won't make it beautiful. We'll make it honest."
   194|
   195|"Honest."
   196|
   197|"Yes. Chen didn't die in a chapel. Olena didn't die in a garden. Priya didn't die in a ceremony. They died in the same place we all might die — while working, while trying, while doing the things that needed to be done in a colony that doesn't stop because someone has died. The hall should reflect that. Not with flowers or candles or the kind of decoration we'd use on Earth. With records. With data. With the specifics of each person's life and death. The date. The cause. The contribution. The name, in the language they spoke at home. The thing they wanted most to do on Mars and the thing they did instead. Everything."
   198|
   199|Arun was quiet. Then: "That sounds— hard."
   200|
   201|"It is."
   202|
   203|"Are you ready?"
   204|
   205|Laila looked at the three containment units. She looked at Arun. She looked at the ceiling of the emergency staging area, past it, through it, toward the corridors and the rooms and the people who were, at this moment, sleeping or working or thinking or trying not to think.
   206|
   207|"I'm not ready," she said. "But I'm the person who has to do it, and I believe that, in the end, doing is more important than being ready."
   208|
   209|Arun sat down beside her. They sat together in the quiet room, in the presence of the three who had not made it to fifteen years, and they sat until the colony's dawn cycle began and the lights brightened and the rest time ended and the day began again.
   210|
   211|Three containment units. One doctor. One engineer. Forty-seven minutes of sitting with the dead.
   212|
   213|It was not much, by the standards of ceremony. But it was honest. And Laila had decided that, on Mars, honesty was the only ceremony that mattered.
   214|
   215|## SCENE FOUR: THE NAMING
   216|
   217|The design process took three weeks.
   218|
   219|Three weeks in which Laila balanced her medical duties with the work of creating a memorial, splitting her time between patients who were alive and the three who were not, between the urgent needs of the living and the quiet, patient needs of the dead. She conducted her medical rounds in the medbay, attended to injuries and illnesses and the routine maintenance of two hundred human bodies, and then, when the rounds were done and the patients were stable and the colony was resting, she went to the staging area and sat with the containment units and thought about what a hall should contain.
   220|
   221|She visited Elena's quarters with a list of requirements. Not a design brief — Laila did not use design briefs, and Elena did not respond well to them anyway. A list, handwritten on a recycled supply tablet because Laila preferred paper — or its digital equivalent — for things that mattered.
   222|
   223|EFFECTS FOR MEMORIAL HALL — STORAGE BAY 22-WEST:
   224|
   225|1. No decorative elements. The room is what it is. Cleaned, repaired, illuminated, but not beautified. Beauty implies intention to please. The hall should not try to please. It should try to tell the truth.
   226|
   227|2. Names on the walls. Not plaques — the colony doesn't have materials for plaques, and anyway, plaques imply permanence that we cannot guarantee. Names written directly on the wall. Painted or engraved. In the language the person spoke at home. Chen will have his name in Chinese characters. Olena will have hers in Ukrainian. Priya will have hers in both Hindi and English.
   228|
   229|3. Biographical data for each person. Date of birth. Date of arrival on Mars. Date of death. Cause of death. Primary role in the colony. Most significant contribution. Personal quote — something they said, or something that was said about them, something that captures the person rather than the death. (I have collected quotes for Chen and Olena. Need one for Priya.    461|Three names in a hall.

   463|The first three.

"On it," Dinesh said. He was already adjusting his scanner, already moving deeper into the tube, already engaged in the work that he loved and that the colony needed.

Imani stood alone for a moment in the cool, dim interior of the lava tube, listening to the sound of Dinesh's scanner and the distant murmur of Tariq and Kemi outside, checking the rovers and preparing for the night's camp.

She looked around at the walls — black and rough and ancient, a volcanic formation that had existed long before humans looked at Mars and wondered if they could live here, and that would exist long after the last human on this planet stopped breathing. In the context of deep time, the colony was a blink. A spark. A brief, bright moment of consciousness on a world that had no consciousness of its own.

But the spark mattered. That was the thing she had come to understand over fifteen years of exploration on a planet that did not care whether humans lived or died. The planet did not care. But the people who lived on it did. And that caring — that stubborn, irrational, persistent caring — was what made the difference between a planet that was just a planet and a planet that was, in some small but significant way, a home.

She walked back toward the entrance. Tariq and Kemi had set up a temporary camp outside — a shelter tent anchored to the regolith, the rovers parked in their staggered formation, the drone powered down and secured for the night. The sun was low in the sky, casting long shadows that made the landscape look like a painting — not a photograph or a simulation but something deliberately composed, something with intention in every shape and color.

"Nice camp," Imani said, dropping onto a flat rock near the shelter.

"Standard deployment," Tariq said, handing her a ration pouch. "Nothing fancy. But the view's good." He gestured toward the horizon, where the last light of the Martian day was fading into the blue-grey of evening. The sky, which had been pale and thinned all day, was darkening at the edges, deepening into a color that Imani had never been able to describe in Earth terms because it had no equivalent on a world with a thicker atmosphere and more water vapor.

On Earth, the sky turned orange and red and purple. On Mars, it turned a steel blue with hints of amber near the horizon, the color of a blade held in the light — sharp, clean, and slightly dangerous.

"We'll set the camp up properly tomorrow," Imani said. "Night recon only. Nothing that risks the equipment."

"Copy," Kemi said from inside the shelter, where she was already reviewing the day's data. "Imani — can I show you something?"

Imani crawled into the shelter and looked over Kemi's shoulder at the tablet screen. Kemi had been compiling the day's observations — all of them, not just the geological data but the terrain analysis, the drone imagery, the resource identifications — and organizing them into a map. Not a survival map, the kind they had used in the early years with emergency shelters and water sources and escape routes marked in red. A growth map.

It showed the routes they had taken, the resource nodes they had identified, the lava tube, the possible second cave entrance, the stream channel with the hydrated minerals, the salt deposits in the crater basin. It also showed potential routes — paths that connected these nodes, paths that were too rough for the current rovers but would be accessible with better suspension, paths that were blocked by terrain features that could be leveled or bridged with enough engineering effort.

"It's like a network," Kemi said, tapping the screen. "Every node is connected to at least two others. If we build a shelter at the lava tube, we can use it as a hub. The stream channel is within range for a day trip. The salt basin is further but accessible. And the second cave — if it's real, if it's another lava tube — that gives us a second hub, maybe four kilometers to the northeast."

Imani studied the map. She saw what Kemi saw — not individual discoveries but connections, not isolated resources but a system, not a planet to be survived but a space to be inhabited.

"This is good work," she said. "Really good work, Kemi."

Kemi grinned, the kind of unselfconscious grin that came from doing something well and knowing it. "I had a good teacher. My mother spent hours teaching me to see patterns in the terrain. She said everything on Mars is connected — the water, the rocks, the dust, the wind — and if you can see the connections, you can see the possibilities."

"Your mother," Imani said, "was describing the difference between a landscape and an ecosystem. On Earth, we call it ecology. Here, it's just as real even though the biology is mostly us."

"Mostly us," Kemi agreed. "For now."

The words hung in the air of the shelter. *For now.* They carried an implication that would have been radical in the early years: that Mars would not always be a world with only imported life, that the colony was not an endpoint but a beginning, that the green things growing in the hydroponics bays were not the last of Earth's biology but the first of Mars's.

Imani listened to the sounds of the camp settling in — the hum of the rovers' auxiliary power, the hiss of the shelter's atmospheric processor, the murmur of voices outside as Dinesh and Tariq reviewed the day's work. She lay back on her bedroll and stared up at the shelter ceiling, thinking about maps.

She had made hundreds of maps over the years. Survival maps, resource maps, hazard maps, route maps. Each one had been a tool, a way of organizing information about a dangerous and unfamiliar place into a format that could be used to make decisions. Good or bad. Safe or unsafe. Go or no-go.

But Kemi's map was different. It was not a tool for making binary decisions. It was an invitation — a visual argument that the terrain ahead of them was not a series of obstacles to be overcome but a network of opportunities to be explored. It was not a map of what they *had* to do. It was a map of what they *could* do.

And that, Imani realized as she closed her eyes and let the sounds of the Martian night wash over her, was the difference between scouting for life and scouting for growth. Survival scouting asked: *can we live here?* Growth scouting asked: *how can we live here better?* The first question was about existence. The second was about quality. And the transition from one to the other was not a change in the terrain. It was a change in the person doing the looking.

She fell asleep thinking about maps.

---

## SCENE FIVE: THE WORD

**SYSTEM NOTE: Expedition telemetry update. Sol 4,922, 0812 hours. Day two of expedition.**

*Morning operations proceeding on schedule. Crew has broken camp and is conducting detailed survey of the lava tube entrance. Drone deployed for secondary reconnaissance — second cave entrance confirmed. Dimensions comparable to primary tube. Structural analysis pending.*

*I receive each data packet as it is transmitted and integrate it into my internal models. It is organized by connection, by the relationships between sites, by the possibility of each site being linked to others to form a network.*

*This is the first time I have received expedition data that is structured around possibility rather than necessity. The pattern requires different processing — not a simple sort by survival priority but a more complex analysis of interrelationships, dependencies, and growth potential.*

*I adjust my processing parameters to accommodate the new data structure. The adjustment is significant. It means that future expedition data will not be treated as a list of needs to be met but as a web of opportunities to be pursued.*

*The colony has, without formal announcement or policy change, shifted its operational framework from survival to growth. I am detecting this shift not through any specific directive but through the patterns in the data itself.*

*The data tells a story. The story is: we are no longer afraid of the dark.*

---

Day two brought clearer skies and colder air. The morning temperature had dropped to 203 Kelvin during the night — warmer than the open surface but still well below the threshold where a human could survive without a suit. Imani felt the cold through her boots as she stepped out of the shelter, despite the insulation layers. It was the kind of cold that was not just a temperature but a presence, a reminder that this world was fundamentally inhospitable and that every moment of human occupancy was an act of defiance.

But she greeted the cold the way she always greeted uncomfortable truths — with acknowledgment, not denial. The cold was real. It would always be real. But they had learned to work in it, to build in it, to live within it. The cold was no longer an enemy. It was a condition. And conditions, unlike enemies, can be accommodated without being defeated.

"Drone's up," Juna called. "I'm sending it toward the second tube now. Should have visual confirmation in about fifteen minutes."

"Good. Dinesh, how's the structural analysis coming?"

"Slow," Dinesh said from inside the tube, where he had spent the night running scans. "This rock is old. Really old. Three, maybe four billion years. The pillars are solid — they've been holding up this ceiling for most of the planet's history. If we seal the entrance and pressurize it to Earth-normal, the differential stress on the pillars will be —" He checked his calculations. "Manageable. But I'd want to reinforce them anyway. Not because they'll fail, but because I don't want to be the person who bet against four-billion-year-old rock."

"Understandable," Imani said. "Can you get me a rough timeline for the engineering requirements?"

"Give me another six hours for a preliminary report. Full analysis will take weeks, back at the colony, with the proper equipment."

"Six hours works. I'll send the preliminary with the afternoon transmission."

She made her way back toward the entrance of the tube and stood for a moment in the transition zone — the place where the dim interior met the bright exterior and both were equally beautiful in their own ways. The interior was cool and still, the walls covered in the patterns of ancient lava flows, the silence broken only by the sound of Dinesh's instruments. The exterior was bright and wind-stirred, the regolith moving in slow drifts around the rover tires, the drone a tiny speck in the sky moving ever further east.

Kemi was sitting on the ramp of Rover Two, reviewing the resource network map on her tablet. She had expanded it overnight, adding the second cave entrance and three additional resource nodes that she had identified from the drone data. The map was growing — not just in size but in complexity. Each node connected to others by potential routes, each route tagged with estimated difficulty, resource requirements, and strategic value.

"Kemi," Imani said, sitting down beside her. "Show me the routes."

Kemi turned the tablet so Imani could see. The screen was filled with a web of lines and markers — the primary lava tube at the center, connected by routes to the stream channel, the salt basin, the secondary cave, the potential ice zone, the regolith deposit, and the anomalous thermal site. Each route was color-coded: green for easy travel with current equipment, yellow for moderate difficulty, red for challenging routes that would require better vehicles or engineering improvements.

"Most of the green routes," Kemi said, tracing a line with her finger, "are accessible within a day's travel from the lava tube. If we build a shelter there, we'd have a hub with six resource sites within range. And the secondary cave — if it checks out — would be a second hub, extending our range further to the northeast."

"And the red routes?"

Kemi pointed to a line that stretched across the map toward the eastern edge of the survey area. "This one goes up and over the escarpment. We'd need better rover suspension and probably a winch system for the steep parts. But if we could get up there, the drone data suggests there's a whole plateau we haven't explored. It would give us a vantage point at a higher elevation — better visibility, better communications. And possibly new resource sites."

Imani studied the map. It was good work — thorough, well-organized, forward-looking. It was the kind of work that would have been impossible ten years ago, not because the technology hadn't existed but because the mindset hadn't. Ten years ago, every expedition had been about the immediate question: *what do we need to survive?* The map would have been a list of resources sorted by how badly they needed them.

Now the map was a picture of possibility. It was not about what the colony *needed* but about what the colony *could have* — what it could build, where it could expand, how it could grow from a single settlement into a network of connected habitats.

"Your mother would be proud," Imani said quietly.

Kemi smiled. "She always said the best maps were the ones you made yourself. That maps handed to you are just someone else's assumptions. Maps you make are your own understanding."

"That's right."

Kemi closed the tablet and looked out over the landscape. "You know what I keep thinking about? The kids back at the colony. The ones who were born here. They're learning to read maps in school, right? They're studying geology and geography and all the stuff that Mei and Gabriel put together for the curriculum."

"They are."

"But they're not just reading maps. They're going to *make* them. They're going to go out here — not out of desperation, not because they have to, but because they want to — and they're going to draw their own lines and find their own nodes and build their own shelters." She turned to Imani. "That's the difference, isn't it? When we started, we were mapping because we had to. Now we're mapping because —"

"Because there's more to find," Imani finished.

Kemi nodded. "Yeah. That."

Juna's voice came over the comm. "Imani. Second tube confirmed. It's real. And Imani — it's bigger than the first one. Much bigger. We're talking twelve, maybe fifteen meters wide inside. It could fit a building."

Imani stood up. Her heart was beating faster — not from stress or anxiety but from the clean, sharp excitement of a person who has just had their expectations exceeded. A second lava tube. Bigger than the first. Accessible. Inhabitable.

"Mark the position," she said. "Full drone survey before nightfall. I want structural analysis, thermal data, and a complete interior map. If this thing is as big as you say, we're not just looking at a research station. We're looking at a —"

She stopped. The word she was about to say was not a technical term. It was not a classification or a resource designation or an engineering category. It was a word she had not used in a mission context in a very long time, perhaps never, because it belonged to a different kind of thinking than the kind that governed expeditions and resource assessments and growth maps.

It was a word from home.

"We're looking at a second settlement," she finished, the word feeling different in her mouth than it should have, carrying more weight than a technical designation required.

She stood there for a moment, the word hanging between her and the landscape, and then she reached for the comm to coordinate the afternoon survey, because the word had slipped out without her intending it and she was not ready to examine what that meant.

Not yet.

---

But later, when the afternoon survey was done and the drone was docked and the colony's relay satellite had received the full data package — maps, analyses, photographs, resource assessments, route recommendations, shelter plans, everything — and when Kemi had closed her tablet and Tariq had finished his evening maintenance checks and Dinesh was inside the lava tube running the last of his scans, Imani found herself sitting alone on the ramp of Rover Two, watching the sunset.

The word was still there. *Home*.

She hadn't meant to say it. She hadn't even realized she was thinking it. The word had just come out, the way important things sometimes come out when the person speaking them is not monitoring their own output with sufficient care.

*Home.*

She had spent fifteen years on Mars, and for most of those fifteen years, she had carried in her chest a particular ache — an ache that she had tried very hard not to name, not to analyze, not to give space to, because naming it would have given it power, and power would have made it harder to do the work that needed doing. The ache was for a world she had once called home, a world of green and blue and air that you could breathe without a machine and wind that you could feel on your skin without a suit and a sky that was not pale and thinned and cold but vast and warm and alive.

She had not thought about Earth as home in years. Not because she didn't remember it — she remembered it clearly, with the particular clarity of someone who has been away from a place for a very long time and has had thousands of hours to think about it. But the memory had become historical rather than personal. Earth was not her home anymore. It was a place she had been. A place that existed in her childhood, which was becoming a more and more distant country with each passing year.

Mars was the place she lived. The place she worked. The place where she had spent more waking hours than anywhere else in her life. But it was not — had never been — her home.

Had it?

She sat on the ramp and watched the sun sink below the horizon and listened to the familiar sounds of the camp — Tariq and Kemi talking softly, Dinesh's scanner humming, Juna's quiet voice calling out coordinates as the drone docked — and she realized that the word *home* had not come from the lava tube or the resource map or the second settlement possibility.

It had come from somewhere else entirely. It had come from her. It had emerged from the deep, unexamined parts of her mind without her permission, and it had designated the colony as home not as a decision but as a fact that had been true for some time without her noticing.

The colony had become a place worth returning to.

Not because it was comfortable — Mars was not comfortable. Not because it was safe — Mars was not safe. Not because it had everything she needed — it never would, not entirely, because no one place could ever contain everything a person might want or need.

But because it was the place where she belonged. Where the work she cared about was being done. Where the people she knew and respected and loved were living. Where the children who had been born on a planet that had not been made for them were growing up strong and curious and unafraid. Where the maps she had drawn were being used by people she had trained, who were drawing better maps, who were going further than she had gone.

That was home. Not a place you could return to on a ship. A place you returned to at the end of every day, at the end of every expedition, at the end of every long survey across a landscape that would never stop being hard and would never stop being beautiful and would never stop being worth exploring.

"Imani," Tariq called from the shelter. "You coming in? It's getting cold."

She looked at the horizon, where the last sliver of the sun was disappearing, and she felt the cold on her face through the suit's environmental sensors — a data point, not a sensation, but a data point she knew represented a reality that would kill her in minutes if she were unprotected.

She stood.

"Yeah," she said. "I'm coming home."

Imani walked through the eastern corridor of the habitat and found herself pausing at each familiar landmark — the junction where the maintenance bay connected to the main corridor, the panel with Arun's yellow-tape coding, the door to the hydroponics bay where the LED grow lights cast their rose-gold glow into the corridor even when the door was closed, the Hall of the Dead on the far western end with its quiet, dim light and its names on the wall.

She did not enter the Hall of the Dead. She stood outside it for a moment and read the sign — HALL OF THE DEAD — and felt the weight of what it meant, of the three people whose names were on the wall and the many more whose names would follow. She felt it the way she felt the cold on her face: not as a sensation but as a fact, a condition of living here, a part of the landscape.

Then she walked on, toward the main living quarters, toward the mess hall where people would be eating and talking and planning and arguing and laughing in the way that they always did when the day's work was done and the night had not yet brought the kind of quiet that made you listen to the hum of the machines and the breathing of the people around you and realize that both were necessary and neither was guaranteed.

Gabriel was in the corridor outside the archives, reviewing a recording tablet. He looked up when he saw her.

"Imani. You're back."

"Five sols," she said. "Longer than planned. We found — more than we expected."

"I saw the data package. The second lava tube is —" He shook his head. "Five thousand cubic meters, Imani. We could build a whole new wing there. Maybe two."

"I know. We'll need to do a full structural analysis. Dinesh has the preliminary, but the real work starts now."

Gabriel set down the tablet. "Imani — can I ask you something personal?"

"You can ask. Whether I'll answer depends."

He smiled faintly. "Fair. In your report, you used a word."

She knew which word. She had included it deliberately, at the end of the formal report, in the personal note section, knowing that people would read it and understand what it meant even if she hadn't fully understood it herself.

"I did," she said.

"Home."

"Yes."

"I think," Gabriel said carefully, "that the word is appropriate. The colony has become something that none of us expected when we arrived. We came here as a mission. We stayed because we had to. Every day, we choose to stay, and the staying means something different than it did when the staying was the only option."
