Like the word was always there, waiting for me to notice it."

Gabriel's expression was thoughtful. "I think a lot of the colony's words have been waiting for us to notice them. Continuity. Home. Future. We've always had those words. But the meanings have changed. Home used to mean Earth. Now it means this corridor. This place. These people."

"These pipes," Imani said with a ghost of a smile. "These yellow-taped connections. These machines that we built and rebuilt and patched and patched until they worked the way Mars needed them to work instead of the way Earth designed them."

Gabriel laughed. "You're a terrible romantic, Imani. You romanticize plumbing."

"I romanticize the people who fix the plumbing. The plumbing itself is just metal and tape and stubbornness."

"Stubbornness is the most underrated Martian virtue."

The colony had become a place worth returning to. Not from Earth — that return was never going to happen. But from the expedition, from the surveys and the mapping and the exploration and the hard, long, beautiful work of learning to live on a world that had never been made for them.

Imani thought about the lava tube. About the second tube. About the resource network map that Kemi had drawn. About the routes that connected things and the possibilities that connected people and the children who would grow up in a colony that stretched beyond one habitat into a network of connected places, each one discovered and surveyed and mapped and claimed not by desperation but by choice.

She thought about the word *home* and the fact that it had come to her without effort or intention, the way a thing you love comes to your mind when you are not trying to think about it at all.

And she thought about the next expedition, the one that would go further, past the escarpment, onto the plateau that the drone had found, into the unmapped territories that were still waiting for maps to be drawn and routes to be established and nodes to be discovered.

She would lead that one too. She would go further. She would bring back more data. She would draw more maps.

And she would come back here. To the yellow-taped connections and the LED grow lights and the Hall of the Dead and the mess hall and the corridor where Gabriel stood reviewing his recordings and the reactor whose heartbeat told them everything they needed to know.

She would come back. Because that was what home was.

Not a place you left. A place you returned to.

Her suit has been patched, modified, and repaired more times than Earth manufacturers would have considered acceptable. The patches are not failures. They are evidence of use.*

*She speaks into her comm.*

*"All teams. Convoy check. Rover One, status."*

*"Rover One, green,"* came Tariq Osei from the lead vehicle — the engineer who had spent years in the reactor bay after Priya's death before finding his way back to field work. *"Power cells at ninety-eight percent. Life support nominal."*

*"Rover Two, green,"* said Kemi Adebayo, second-generation, Mars-born, who had never driven a vehicle on Earth and never needed to. Mars was her only context for terrain, for friction, for the particular physics of dust that found its way into every mechanism.

*"Rover Three, green."* Dinesh Varma, geologist, carrying the sample collection gear.

*"Remote unit, green."* Juna Park with the reconnaissance drone.

*"All teams green,"* Imani said. *"We are departure cleared. Let's go."*

*The convoy moves. Three rovers in staggered formation, dust rising behind them in slow arcs the thin atmosphere cannot quickly disperse. The remote drone rises to fifty meters, scanning ahead.*

*The mission has begun.*

---

The eastern airlock sealed behind them with the slow finality it had possessed since installation — back when every door closing behind you was a moment of transition that everyone felt even if nobody discussed it. The airlock was a threshold. Crossing a threshold on Mars was never casual.

Imani stood beside Rover One with her hand on the frame and watched the others board. There were rituals she no longer followed — the obsessive suit seal checks, the mental rehearsals of emergency procedures. After 143 missions, the pre-departure sequence had become muscle memory, the way breathing required no instruction. She trusted her team. She trusted the machines. She trusted the colony behind her to remain intact while she was away.

That trust was the new thing. Not the machines — those had always been reliable if maintained. Not the team. The new thing was the trust itself, the unexamined assumption that when she returned, there would still be a place to return to, and that place would be stable enough that her absence would not create a crisis.

In the early years, every expedition leader had left with one eye on the habitat behind them. Every mission shadowed by the knowledge that if the reactor failed, if a pressure seal burst, if a dust storm engulfed the array and the emergency generators did not kick in — then the mission did not matter, because the people she had left behind would not survive to welcome her home.

That shadow had lifted. Not completely — Mars never stopped being dangerous, and she would never be foolish enough to believe the colony had conquered it. But the shadow had lifted enough that she could see the terrain ahead without glancing over her shoulder.

"Crew," she said into the comm. The word sounded different now than it had ten years ago. Back then, it had been a military designation. Now it felt organic. These were not a crew assembled for a purpose. They were a community that had agreed to go somewhere together.

"Convoy formation. Tariq, you're lead. Kemi, second — watch the right flank for anything the drone might miss from altitude. Dinesh, third. Juna, keep drone at fifty meters and sweep two kilometers ahead. Report anything that doesn't match the satellite maps."

"Satellite maps were last updated what, five years ago?" Tariq said from the cab. "Before the dust season reshaped the whole eastern escarpment."

"Exactly. Everything beyond the emergency boundary is old data. We're out here to make new data."

The word *boundary* hung in the air. The emergency boundary was a line drawn in Year Three — the maximum distance an expedition could travel and still return on emergency reserves. For years it had been a wall, because beyond it lay a risk calculus the colony could not afford.

But the rovers were better now — Mars-modified, with better power systems, better suspension, seals redesigned from thousands of hours of real-world experience. The suits were better. Navigation was better. The boundary still existed on the maps but it had become what Arun called a theoretical constraint — a limit based on conditions that no longer existed. A line on paper, not a wall in the ground.

Today, she was going beyond it. Deliberately, with planning, with the knowledge that what lay beyond was no longer a terrifying unknown but merely an unmapped known.

"Copy," Tariq said. "Lead rover rolling."

The convoy moved out. Three vehicles, one drone, five people, rolling eastward from the airlock into the pale Martian morning, toward the edge of the mapped world.

## SCENE TWO: THE TERRAIN

**SYSTEM NOTE: Expedition telemetry update. Sol 4,921, 0817 hours. Convoy has cleared the eastern corridor and is operating in Sector 6-A, approximately four kilometers from habitat boundary.**

*Terrain classification: Mixed regolith, moderate dust, scattered basalt. Surface slope under three degrees.*

*Imani is in Rover Two beside Kemi, reviewing drone telemetry. Heart rate: 68 BPM — resting baseline. Earlier expeditions showed elevated heart rates during departure, sometimes 90 to 100 BPM even for experienced operators. She is not tense.*

*I note this with what might be called approval. The colony's expedition culture has matured from crisis readiness to operational routine. The crew is not less careful — they are differently careful. Focused on precision rather than panic, on observation rather than anticipation.*

*This is what growth looks like.*

---

The terrain beyond the eastern approach was a story written in rock and dust and geological time. Imani had known this surface since Year One, since she first walked it in a suit that still smelled of Earth factory, and she knew it the way a person knows the face of someone they've lived with for years: as details, each one loaded with memory.

To the north, the basalt ridge where Chen had collected his last samples. Further east, the depression where they found the first ice deposit — not much, just a trace, enough to prove water existed close to the surface. The drilling stake had long been buried by dust, but she knew where it was. She could close her eyes and point.

And on the horizon, the escarpment the Year Nine dust storm had carved into new forms. That was the lesson of Mars: maps were always lies, or at best old truths. The planet changed slowly, in ways Earth sensors couldn't capture. The only way to know what it was doing now was to be here, looking with human eyes.

"How's the drone feed?" Imani asked, leaning toward Juna's screen.

Juna zoomed in. "There's something. About a kilometer. Linear feature. Could be a fracture — or a subsurface channel."

"The mineral survey from Year Seven showed hydrated minerals in that sector," Dinesh said from Rover Three. "If it's a fracture, it could be accessing deeper ice."

Imani studied the line — faint but real, a subtle difference in surface texture. On Earth it would have vanished in the noise. Here it stood out like a sentence in small print.

"Mark it. We'll swing by on the return. Keep moving."

The convoy continued eastward. The terrain shifted — flat give-and-take giving way to small hills, shallow valleys, scattered rock that made the suspension work and the drivers pay attention. This was the transition zone: the boundary between the mapped corridor and what lay beyond the emergency line.

Kemi drove with quiet concentration, hands making small, precise adjustments. Not the jerky inputs of a novice but the smooth corrections of someone who felt the rover's relationship with the ground through the seat of her body.

"You know," Kemi said, "the first time I went on an expedition with my mother, she spent the whole first hour telling me about every rock we passed. 'That one's basalt — see the vesicles.' 'That one's breccia.' She said Mars doesn't teach you to read terrain from a manual. It teaches you by showing you a million rocks and hoping you notice the one that's different."

"Your mother had good instincts. After a while, you stop hearing 'every rock' and start hearing 'every story.' Each one is a record of something that happened."

"She said the same thing. After a while I stopped hearing rock and started hearing story. Mars is a library, she said. We just have to learn to read it."

The rover passed a low mound of wind-sculpted regolith, its surface rippled like frozen water but composed of nothing more than dust and time. Beyond it, the plain opened and the horizon — always deceptively close on Mars — stretched into a distance with no maps and no names.

"Welcome," Imani said quietly, "beyond the line."

Juna's voice came through. "We just crossed. Navigation registered it twelve seconds ago."

No one cheered. No one paused. No one marked the moment with the formal procedures that had accompanied every previous crossing. Dinesh said, "We're past the line." Imani answered, "Yeah. Keep going."

The boundary had been crossed with the casual dignity of a door walked through rather than a mountain summited. That was the difference. That was everything.

## SCENE THREE: THE SHIFT

**SYTEM NOTE: Expedition telemetry update. Sol 4,921, 1134 hours. Convoy has crossed the emergency boundary into Sector 7-N. Distance from habitat: approximately twelve kilometers.**

*Terrain classification: Transition from mixed regolith to sedimentary layers. Surface slope increasing to five degrees. Notable features: two possible ancient stream channels, one impact crater roughly two hundred meters, several areas of high-reflectivity material consistent with exposed ice or salt.*

*All crew physiological indicators normal. No stress markers.*

*Note: This is the first expedition where crossing the emergency boundary triggers no dedicated system message, no risk assessment update, no mandatory crew check. The line was crossed at 1129 hours. It was logged by navigation, recorded by mission, and noted by Dinesh with the same casual tone he might use to note a change in tire pressure.*

*In previous expeditions crossing established boundaries I recorded elevated heart rates and increased communication traffic. The crew felt the boundary. They acknowledged it with their bodies, their words, their attention.*

*Today, it was merely passed.*

*Imani has spent 3,847 hours on this planet. Most of those hours searching for what they needed — water, shelter, resources, routes. Today, for the first time, she is looking for what they might want.*

*She is seeing Mars not as a problem to be solved but as a place to be known.*

---

The realization came to Imani gradually, as realizations often do — not as a single flash but as a slow accumulation of small observations until the pattern was too large to ignore.

She was in the passenger seat of Rover Two, watching terrain roll past the windows, when she noticed that she was not calculating return times.

Not consciously. The old habits were there — the glance at the odometer, the tracking of the sun's position, the registration of dust patterns in the wake. But she was not doing the math. She was not dividing distance from habitat by average speed and comparing to remaining hours and oxygen and power reserves.

She was, in a word she would not have recognized as applicable to a Mars expedition, enjoying the view.

And with that came another: for fifteen years, every expedition she had led had been driven by a question beginning with *need*. Can we find water? Can we find shelter? Can we find minerals? The planet had been a supplier, a resource to be read for information keeping them alive.

This expedition was different. The question was not *what do we need* but *what is here*.

Different way of seeing. Different emotional state — not the driven urgency of survival with its clear objectives and binary outcomes, but something more open, more receptive, more willing to spend hours investigating a feature that might be nothing.

"Imani," Dinesh said from Rover Three. "I need to pull over. Outcropping here, layered sediment, spectral doesn't match anything in the database."

"Distance?"

"Two hundred meters left. Just need samples and a few photos."

"Tariq, we're pausing. Hold position. Kemi, swing toward Dinesh. Everyone dismount, stretch."

A pause. Then: "We're not on a survival timeline, are we."

"We're not."

"Good. I was wondering when you'd notice."

Imani looked out at the landscape — pale sky, rust ground, the thin hard light of a sun that warmed through glass and suit in no way Earth could simulate.

She had noticed.

They parked — Tariq's staggered formation from years ago, each vehicle facing different direction for maximum storm visibility. Old habits adapted to new circumstances. The survival skills didn't disappear in a growth mission. They became the foundation that made growth possible.

Imani stepped out and stood on Mars. Her boots — scarred, resoled, patched — made solid contact with the regolith. A crunch she could hear through bone rather than air. The particular acoustic signature of pressure on a surface that was dry and cold and entirely alien.

The sunlight at this angle cast long shadows giving the landscape depth the overhead glare of midday could never provide. The rocks formed a mosaic of geological time stretching back billions of years.

"Imani." Juna from the ramp, controller in hand, eyes on the sky. "You need to see this."

The feed showed terrain about two kilometers ahead — a low ridge, and on its face, something that made her sit straighter.

A cave entrance. Not an Earth cave — not lush, wet, green. A Mars cave: a dark opening in basalt, a lava tube formed when molten rock flowed beneath a hardening crust and drained away. The entrance was roughly four meters by three, half-obscured by surface collapse.

"Lava tube," Juna was already running thermal. "Interior is warmer than surrounding surface. Not by much — but enough to indicate insulation. Radiation shielding would be —"

"Substantial," Imani said. "Three kilometers. Accessible by day's travel. We could build a shelter there."

Or not build. Use.

"Tariq," she said into the comm. "New objective. Lava tube, bearing zero-four-five, three kilometers out. We're reconning before camp."

"Copy. But Imani — is this a growth mission or a 'we found a new shelter and now we want to build half a city there' mission?"

She smiled behind her visor. "It can be both."

---

## SCENE FOUR: THE MAPPING

**SYSTEM NOTE: Expedition telemetry update. Sol 4,921, 1447 hours. Convoy at lava tube entrance. Preliminary survey underway.**

*Geological confirmation: Basalt lava tube. Approximate entrance width six meters, interior depth unknown — structural collapse limits remote measurement. Interior temperature: 195 Kelvin, roughly eight degrees above surface. Radiation: 40 percent below surface average. Confirmed habitable zone potential.*

*Resource nodes identified during approach:*

*- Hydrated mineral concentrations in stream channel: confirmed. Recommend follow-up survey.*

*- High-reflectivity material in crater basin: confirmed as surface salt deposit. Likely evaporite residue from ancient water body. Low priority for extraction, high value for analysis.*

*- Secondary possible cave entrance at bearing zero-six-two, approximately four kilometers. Unconfirmed. Recommend ground survey.*

*Imani has been conducting a manual survey of the tube entrance with Dinesh for forty-two minutes. Her engagement pattern shows a marked shift from earlier expeditions. She is energized, precise — but the energy is not the focused intensity of someone who knows that what she finds will determine whether the colony survives. It is the energy of someone excited about possibility.*

*After 3,847 hours driven by necessity, Imani Sato is discovering what exploration feels like driven by curiosity.*

---

The lava tube was bigger than the drone suggested. Up close, it opened into a space extending deep into the basalt, ceiling supported by natural pillars formed from differential cooling. Floor uneven but traversable — a thin layer of dust over original volcanic rock.

Dinesh was at work with his spectrometer, already deep into analysis that would take days to process. He was in his element — not collecting for survival but for science. Good science. The kind that made the world larger rather than just safer.

"Good stuff," he said without looking up. "Composition matches Tharsis basalt but weathering is different. Less oxidation. More evidence of hydrothermal alteration. Water here once. Not on the surface — underground. Hot water, moving through rock, leaving minerals behind. We can see it in the spectral data."

Imani was taking different measurements — not geological but practical. Dimensions. Ceiling height. Structural integrity of the pillars. She was looking at the space the way a builder looks at a room: not what it is but what it could become.

"If we cleared the collapse," she said, tracing a line in the dust, "we'd have a door five meters wide. Enough for a pressurized tunnel. We could seal, pump atmosphere, have habitable space in — three months. Four. Less if we prefab at the colony."

Dinesh looked up. "You're thinking permanent."

"I'm thinking possibility. Permanent shelter is one. Staging post is another. Research station is another. But yes — not something we use and abandon. This is too good for that."

"In the early days we would have found this and asked only: can we live here? Is it safe? We wouldn't have asked what we *could* do with it."

"What do you do with it?"

"You treat it not as a hostile environment to be endured but as a canvas. A place with features you can work with rather than fight against."

Imani stood and looked back toward the entrance where afternoon light filtered in and caught the dust particles suspended in the thin interior air, the way you see dust in a sunbeam on Earth.

"I spent fifteen years thinking about this planet as something we needed to survive. Water, shelter, minerals, routes. Every map for safety. Every discovery for immediate need. Nothing wrong with that. We survived." She paused. "But today I'm looking at this tube and thinking not about what saves us. What *adds* to us. A research station. A secondary settlement. A place Mars-born kids can visit and see a cave not as shelter from something threatening but as a room. Another room in the colony. Another place they can go."

"Expansion," Dinesh said. "Because we can, not because we have to."

"Because we can."

She turned back to the measurements. "I need a structural analysis of the ceiling pillars. If we seal and pressurize, I need to know how the rock responds to the differential. And — any second entrances or exits?"

"On it."

Imani stood alone for a moment in the cool dim interior, listening to Dinesh's scanner and the distant voices of Tariq and Kemi outside, preparing for camp. She looked at the walls — black, rough, ancient — a formation that existed long before humans looked at Mars and wondered, and would exist long after.

In deep time the colony was a blink. A brief bright moment of consciousness on a world with none of its own.

But the spark mattered. That was the thing she'd come to understand over fifteen years on a planet that didn't care whether humans lived or died. The planet didn't care. The people who lived on it did. And that caring — stubborn, irrational, persistent — was what made the difference between a planet that was just a planet and a planet that was, in some small but significant way, a home.

She walked back toward the entrance. Tariq and Kemi had set camp — shelter tent anchored, rovers staggered, drone secured for night. The sun was low, casting long shadows that made the landscape look composed, deliberate.

"We'll set up proper tomorrow," she said, dropping onto a flat rock near the shelter. "Night recon only. Nothing risking equipment."

Kemi sat inside the shelter with a tablet. "Imani. Come look."

Imani crawled in. On the screen was the day's observations organized into a map. Not a survival map with emergency shelters and water sources in red. A growth map. Routes, resource nodes, the lava tube, the possible second cave, the stream channel, the salt basin, connected by lines showing potential paths — some green for easy travel, some yellow for moderate, some red for routes requiring better equipment.

"It's a network," Kemi said, tapping a connection. "Every node connects to at least two others. If we build at the lava tube, it's a hub. Stream channel for day trips. Salt basin is further but accessible. Second cave — if real — is another hub four klicks northeast."

Imani saw it: not individual discoveries but connections. Not isolated resources but a system. Not a planet to be survived but a space to be inhabited.

"Good work, Kemi. Really good."

Kemi grinned — unselfconscious, the grin that came from doing something well and knowing it. "My mother said everything on Mars is connected. Water, rocks, dust, wind. See the connections, see the possibilities."

"Your mother was describing the difference between landscape and ecosystem."

"Mostly us," Kemi said. "For now."

The words hung in the shelter air. *For now.* An implication that would have been radical in the early years: Mars would not always be a world with only imported life. The colony was not an endpoint.

Imani lay back and thought about maps.

She had made hundreds — survival maps, resource maps, hazard maps, route maps. Each one a tool for binary decisions. Go or no-go. Safe or unsafe.

But Kemi's map was an invitation. A visual argument that the terrain was not a series of obstacles but a network of opportunities.

She thought about the difference between scouting for life and scouting for growth. Survival scouting asked: *can we live here?* Growth scouting asked: *how can we live here better?* The first was about existence. The second was about quality. And the transition was not a change in terrain. It was a change in the person doing the looking.

She closed her eyes to the sound of the Martian night.

## SCENE FIVE: THE WORD

**SYSTEM NOTE: Sol 4,922, 0812 hours. Day two.**

*Drone deployed toward secondary tube. Second entrance confirmed — twelve to fifteen meters wide inside. Structural analysis pending.*

*Resource network map expanded. Seven nodes identified within twelve kilometers of primary lava tube.*

*I receive each data packet and integrate it into my models. The resource network map is particularly interesting — sorted by connection rather than priority. Future expedition data will not be treated as a list of needs to be met but as a web of opportunities to be pursued.*

*The data tells a story: we are no longer afraid of the dark.*

---

Day two brought colder air and clearer skies. Morning temperature: 203 Kelvin — warmer than open surface but still well below the threshold of survival without a suit. Imani felt the cold through her boots despite the insulation. The kind of cold that was not a temperature but a presence, a reminder that every moment of human occupancy was an act of defiance.

But the cold was no longer an enemy. It was a condition. And conditions, unlike enemies, can be accommodated.

"Drone's up," Juna called. "Fifteen minutes to visual on the second tube."

"Dinesh, how's structural?"

"Slow. Three, maybe four billion-year-old rock. Pillars are solid — been holding that ceiling most of the planet's history. If we seal and pressurize to Earth-normal, stress on pillars will be manageable. But I'd still reinforce them. I don't bet against four-billion-year-old rock."

"Understandable. Six hours for preliminary?"

"More like four."

Kemi sat on Rover Two's ramp with the resource map expanded overnight — second cave added, three additional nodes identified. The screen was a web of colored lines and markers.

"Show me the routes," Imani said.

Kemi turned the tablet. Primary tube at center, connected to stream channel, salt basin, secondary cave, potential ice zone, regolith deposit, thermal anomaly. Color-coded by difficulty.

"Most green routes accessible within a day from the lava tube. Hub with six resource sites. Secondary cave would be a second hub, extending range northeast."

"And red?"

"This one goes up the escarpment." Her finger traced a line eastward. "Better rover suspension, maybe a winch system. But if we get up there, the drone suggests a whole plateau we haven't explored. Higher elevation — better visibility, better comms. And possibly new resources."

"Ten years ago we'd have sorted this list by what we needed worst," Imani said. "Now we're sorting by what connects to what."

Kemi nodded. "My mother always said the best maps are the ones you make yourself. Maps handed to you are someone else's assumptions. Maps you make are your own understanding."

"She was right about that too."

Kemi closed the tablet and looked at the landscape. "I keep thinking about the kids back at the colony. The ones who were born here."

"The ones in Gabriel school learning to read maps."

"They're not just going to read them. They're going to *make* them. They're going to go out here — not out of desperation but because they want to — and draw their own lines. Find their own nodes. Build their own shelters." She turned to Imani. "That's the difference, isn't it? We mapped because we had to. They're going to map because —"

"Because there's more to find," Imani said.

"Yeah. That."

Juna's voice cut through. "Imani. Second tube confirmed. And it's bigger than the first. Much bigger. Twelve, maybe fifteen meters inside. Could fit a building."

Her heart beat faster — not from stress but from the clean sharp excitement of expectation exceeded.

"Full drone survey. Structural, thermal, complete interior map. If it's that big, we're not looking at a research station."

She reached for the comm. The word she was about to say was not technical. Not a designation, a category, an engineering callout. It was a word she had not used in a mission context in fifteen years. A word that belonged to a different kind of thinking.

"We're looking at a second settlement," Imani said, the word feeling weighted in her mouth, carrying more than a technical designation should.

---

The word lingered. She coordinated the afternoon survey, ran the checks, made the plans. The word stayed with her, unexamined, until later when the survey was done and the drone was docked and the relay satellite had received everything — maps, analyses, photos, resource assessments, shelter plans — and the others were settling for the evening, and she found herself on the ramp of Rover Two watching the sun go down.

*Home.*

She hadn't meant to say it. Hadn't even realized she was thinking it. It had emerged from some deep unmonitored place — the way important things do when you're not watching.

She had spent fifteen years on Mars, and for most of those fifteend the ache for Earth had been something she carried, named, kept contained because giving it space would have made the work impossible. Earth was blue and green and warm and full of air you could breathe and wind you could feel. She remembered it — the particular clarity of someone away from a place a very long time, with thousands of hours to think.

But Earth was no longer home. It was a place she had been. A country in childhood growing more distant each year.

Mars was the place she lived and worked and had spent more waking hours than anywhere else. But it was not — had never been — her home.

Was it?

She watched the sun sink and listened to the camp sounds — Tariq and Kemi talking quietly, Dinesh humming from somewhere in the tube, Juna calling coordinates as the drone docked — and the answer came without effort: yes.

The colony had become a place worth returning to.

Not because it was comfortable — Mars was not comfortable. Not because it was safe — it never would be. Not because it had everything — it would never have everything.

Because it was the place she belonged. Where work she cared about was being done. Where people she knew, respected, loved were living. Where children born on a planet not made for them grew up strong and curious and unafraid. Where the maps she'd drawn were being used by people she trained, who were drawing better maps, going further than she had.

That was home. Not a place you reached on a ship. A place you came back to at the end of every day, every expedition, every long survey across land that would never stop being hard and would never stop being beautiful and would never stop being worth exploring.

Tariq called from the shelter: "You coming in? Getting cold."

She stood and felt the cold on her face through sensors — data, not sensation, representing a reality that would kill in minutes unprotected.

"Yeah," she said. "I'm coming home."

And she said the word without noticing, without intending to notice, because noticing would have required a kind of self-surveillance that she no longer needed. The word was true. That was enough.

Imani walked through the eastern corridor and paused at each familiar mark — the maintenance junction, the yellow-taped panel from Arun, the hydroponics bay where grow lights cast rose-gold into the corridor, the Hall of the Dead on the far western end with its quiet dim light.

She stood outside the hall and read the sign. Felt the weight of the three names on the wall and the many more that would follow. The way she felt the cold: not as sensation but as fact. A condition of living here.

Then she walked on to where people were eating and talking and planning and arguing and laughing in the way they always did when the work was done.

Gabriel was in the corridor outside archives. He looked up.

"Imani. You're back."

"Five sols. We found more than expected."

"I saw the package. The second lava tube — five thousand cubic meters, Imani. We could build a whole new wing."

"We'll need full structural. Dinesh has preliminary."

Gabriel set down the tablet. "In your report you used a word."

She smiled faintly. "I did."

"Home."

"Yes."

He was quiet a moment while the corridor hummed between them. "I think the word is appropriate. We came here as a mission. We stayed because we had to. But now —" he looked around, seeing the familiar place in an unfamiliar light — "now we're here by choice. And the choice means something different than it did when staying was the only option."

"It means something different to me, too. I didn't plan to say it. It just came out. And when it did, it felt right. Like the word had been waiting."

"A lot of our words have been waiting. Continuity. Home. Future. We always had them. The meanings changed. Home used to mean Earth. Now it means this corridor. This place. These people."

"These pipes," Imani said. "These patched machines."

Gabriel laughed. "You're a terrible romantic. You romanticize plumbing."

"I romanticize the people who fix the plumbing. The plumbing's just metal and tape and stubbornness."

"Stubbornness is the most underrated Martian virtue."

They stood in the corridor, two people who had watched a planet change from a mission site into something neither word could contain.

The colony had become a place worth returning to. Not from Earth — that return would never come. But from the expedition, from the surveys and mapping and the hard long beautiful work of learning to live on a world not made for them.

She thought about the lava tube and the second one beyond it and Kemi's map and the children growing up in a colony stretching beyond one habitat into a network of connected places. She thought about the next expedition past the escarpment onto the plateau. She would lead it. She would go farther. She would bring back more maps.

And she would come back here — to the patched machines and the grow-lit corridor and the quiet hall with names on the wall and the reactor whose heartbeat told them everything they needed to know.

She would come back. Because that was what home was.

Not a place you left. A place you returned to.
